title: A Preregistered Audit of Dataset Contamination Controls in LLM-for-NetOps Benchmarks
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, confirmatory audit to test whether conservative deterministic contamination detectors (exact‑match + fuzzy 5‑gram + provenance heuristics) flag items in a reproducible 150‑item NetOps sample and whether applying preregistered contamination controls changes validator‑based success rates. The preregistered design (study_id = contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1) specified 150 item pairs (baseline vs guarded) evaluated with a single hosted model (declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini") and a deterministic NetOps validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). The executed run sampled provenance‑stable synthetic items using a deterministic generator and used shared_initial_candidate semantics (independent_condition_generation = false). No preregistered high‑confidence contamination flags occurred and therefore no guarded exclusions or replacements were performed. All 150 baseline and matched guarded episodes passed the validator (baseline = 150/150, guarded = 150/150). The paired success‑rate difference = 0.0 percentage points (95% CI [0.0, 0.0]); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Crucially, the execution facts that the sample was synthetic and that a single shared generation per item was reused materially limited the audit's sensitivity to detect generation‑level contamination in this run; we explicitly reconcile preregistration→execution artifacts, explain this degeneracy using archived traces, and provide artifact‑grounded recommendations for audit designs that would be sensitive to contamination in web‑sourced benchmarks.

sections.introduction:
Motivation. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to network operations (NetOps) tasks such as intent‑to‑configuration translation and automated configuration repair. Operational adoption requires that benchmarked performance reflect realistic capabilities rather than artifacts of dataset contamination or templated tasks that leak into model training data. Meta‑analyses and recent work call for contamination‑aware evaluations and validator‑backed oracles to avoid inflated claims of reliability.

Research question and contribution. We preregistered and executed an artifact‑anchored audit to answer: under conservative deterministic contamination detectors (exact normalized token equality; fuzzy 5‑gram shingle overlap with preregistered thresholds; provenance timestamp heuristics) and a guarded exclusion policy, how many high‑confidence flags arise in a reproducible 150‑item NetOps sample, and how much does applying those controls change an LLM's validator pass rate? Our contributions are: (1) a fully preregistered confirmatory experiment (study_id = contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1) executed end‑to‑end and archived; (2) exact, artifact‑verified confirmatory statistics on Npairs = 150 with full deterministic validator traces; and (3) a preregistration→execution reconciliation that identifies why the run produced a degenerate null and prescribes concrete, artifact‑grounded design changes to increase audit sensitivity in future work.

Scope and bounded claims. The audit intentionally targeted a methodological question about preregistered contamination controls, not a prevalence estimate for public web‑sourced benchmarks. As described in Methods and repeated in the Disclosure Statement, the executed confirmatory sample used provenance‑stable synthetic tasks generated by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 and employed shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (independent_condition_generation = false). Because both facts are recorded in the archived task_manifest and model_configuration artifacts, they limit the inferential scope: the observed zero‑flag, zero‑difference outcome applies to this synthetic sampling and generation regime and does not imply absence of contamination in independent public benchmarks.
sections.related_work:
LLM‑driven NetOps systems and validation. Recent system and benchmark papers show that LLMs can produce operationally useful configuration artifacts under constrained settings, and that integrating verifiers or validate–repair loops improves average repair quality compared to naive generation. Frameworks for formal network verification (e.g., Header Space Analysis and localized subspecification) are practical oracles for reachability and policy correctness and are commonly used in produce–validate pipelines.

Evaluation validity, contamination, and measurement risk. Surveys and meta‑evaluations highlight two recurring risks: (a) contamination—benchmark items or templated prompts appearing in model training data can inflate apparent accuracy; and (b) construct invalidity—benchmarks composed of low‑complexity or highly templated tasks may not map to operational difficulty. These critiques motivate our preregistered detectors (exact token equality, fuzzy 5‑gram overlap thresholds, and provenance heuristics) and a conservative guarded replacement rule for high‑confidence flags. Our audit implements a conservative subset of recommended defenses and measures their effect under a reproducible execution contract.

Positioning. Unlike broader benchmarking efforts that measure absolute model capability, our study evaluates whether a specific, preregistered set of contamination controls would have altered validator‑measured success on a reproducible sample under the archived execution semantics. Where prior works emphasize detector design or end‑to‑end agentic repair, our contribution is an artifact‑anchored, preregistered audit protocol and a concrete preregistration→execution reconciliation grounded in archived traces.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and primary estimand. The experiment was preregistered (study_id = contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1; preregistration SHA‑256 recorded in the execution manifest). The primary estimand is the paired success‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) computed across item×model pairs and tested by exact McNemar two‑sided test. We computed a paired bootstrap percentile 95% confidence interval with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729) per the preregistered analysis executor paired_binary_analysis_v1.

Detectors, thresholds, and guarded policy (preregistered). Detectors were: (1) exact normalized token equality after canonicalization; (2) fuzzy 5‑gram shingle overlap (Jaccard/overlap) with preregistered high‑confidence threshold ≥ 0.80 and sensitivity thresholds at 0.65 and 0.50; and (3) provenance timestamp heuristics comparing item timestamps to model cutoff. The guarded policy deterministically excludes only high‑confidence flagged items (exact match OR fuzzy overlap ≥ 0.80) and replaces them using deterministic retemplating and topology‑augmentation from the same generator distribution with fixed seeds; replacements must meet an embedding similarity constraint per preregistration before acceptance. These rules and replacement semantics are archived in transformation_manifest.json.

Sampling, task generation, and critical execution semantics. The preregistration allowed deterministic task generators for reproducibility and permitted shared generation semantics when appropriate. The actual execution used deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 to produce synthetic tasks (source_identifier prefix "synthetic-netops:") for the confirmatory sample. Execution settings set independent_condition_generation = false (shared_initial_candidate semantics): when no high‑confidence exclusions occur, a single shared model generation per item serves both the baseline and guarded episodes. This execution choice was preregistered and is recorded in execution/model_configuration.json. Because no high‑confidence flags occurred, the shared generation semantics reduced model calls to one per item (model_calls_used = 150) rather than two per pair; the execution manifest and deterministic_reconciliation artifact confirm these counts.

Verifiers and scoring. The verification oracle is deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator traces archived). For each episode the validator performs parse→state‑update→property checks and returns a binary pass/fail and detailed validation traces (observed_touched_field_count, required_command_count, violation codes). The preregistered scoring rule for intent→configuration tasks is full_intent_constraint_validation: the generated configuration must produce the intended final state and respect workflow constraints. Scorer identifiers and representative validator traces are archived under execution/scoring.

Planned analyses and sensitivities. The primary confirmatory test was the prespecified paired analysis with the paired bootstrap CI. Prespecified sensitivity analyses included: (a) treating failed model calls as failures; (b) evaluating fuzzy thresholds at 0.50, 0.65, 0.80; and (c) subgrouping by templated vs realistic items via the templating detector. The preregistration included power guidance: a multi‑model design targeted detection of ≈5 percentage‑point paired differences with 80% power at α=0.05; single‑model single‑call designs reduce sensitivity and have larger minimal detectable effects. All analysis parameters and their archived locations are recorded in analysis/analysis_log.jsonl.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and deterministic reconciliation. The execution completed planned_episode_count = 300 episodes (150 item pairs) with completed_episode_count = 300 and failed_episode_count = 0. Because independent_condition_generation = false and no high‑confidence exclusions occurred, model_calls_used = 150 (one shared generation per item). Deterministic_reconciliation confirms complete_pair_count = 150 and provider call accounting consistent with the preregistered execution contract.

Contamination detector outcomes and absence of flags. The preregistered detectors produced zero high‑confidence contamination flags for the executed sample. analysis/contamination_summary.csv contains no flagged episodes (file header only); the artifact SHA‑256 is recorded in the Disclosure Statement. The detector logs in the archive do not include per‑item fuzzy overlap score summaries for the executed sample because the preregistered detector workflow recorded explicit overlap outputs only for episodes that met flagging criteria or required replacement handling; since no episodes reached the high‑confidence threshold, there were no recorded overlap summary aggregates to report. We therefore report the archive‑documented absence of high‑confidence flags rather than deriving or inventing per‑item overlap statistics.

Validator results and confirmatory statistics. The deterministic_netops_validator_v5 returned pass for all baseline episodes (baseline_success_count = 150/150; baseline_success_rate = 1.0) and for all guarded episodes (guarded_success_count = 150/150; guarded_success_rate = 1.0). The paired contingency table is n11 = 150, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv). The primary estimand (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline) = 0.0 percentage points. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. All numerical outcomes and per‑episode validator traces are archived and their artifact SHAs are recorded.

Representative exemplar. A representative archived episode (pair‑000001 / task‑000001) illustrates the artifact structure and the validator outputs. The archived reference answer and normalized_response for task‑000001 are identical: "interface edge1 admin down\ninterface edge1 vlan 30\ninterface edge1 mtu 1600\ninterface edge1 admin up"; the validator returned score = 1 (score_reason_code = VALID_CONFIGURATION) and provided a validator_trace with final_state and parsed_command_count = 4. This exemplar and its raw response/trace are present under execution/responses and execution/scoring and are referenced by their SHAs in the archived manifest.

Absence of fuzzy‑overlap score summaries and what that means. The preregistered fuzzy‑overlap detector would have produced per‑item overlap scores and flagged episodes if overlaps met preregistered thresholds. In this execution the detector produced no high‑confidence flags and therefore the contamination_summary artifact is empty of flagged rows; the archived detector logs do not contain an aggregated distribution of overlap scores to report here. This is an explicit, artifact‑grounded absence: the archive documents that the detector produced no flags and recorded no replacement operations for the sampled items.
sections.discussion:
Why the result is degenerate (artifact‑grounded explanation). Two archived execution facts explain the degenerate null outcome. First, the sampled items were provenance‑stable synthetic tasks generated by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 (source_identifier prefix "synthetic-netops:"), so canonicalized exact matches to public corpus fingerprints and high fuzzy 5‑gram overlaps above the preregistered high‑confidence threshold did not occur. Second, execution semantics set independent_condition_generation = false (shared_initial_candidate), so when no exclusions were triggered a single shared generation per item was reused for both baseline and guarded episodes. Both facts are recorded in model_configuration.json and task_manifest.jsonl (SHAs referenced in the Disclosure Statement) and together mechanistically produced identical baseline and guarded outputs per item, making the paired comparison uninformative for generation‑level contamination detection in this run.

What this execution answers and what it does not. The archived evidence answers the preregistered methodological question for the executed sampling regime: given provenance‑stable synthetic sampling and conservative deterministic detectors, do high‑confidence flags arise and do deterministic guarded exclusions alter validator pass rates? For this sample and settings the answer is no. The result does not generalize to web‑sourced public benchmarks, to paraphrase‑sensitive contamination, to independent re‑generation semantics, to other LLM families or sizes, or to designs that include multi‑model sampling. We explicitly avoid extrapolating beyond the archive‑supported conclusions.

Design lessons and concrete recommendations grounded in the archive. The preregistration and execution artifacts together imply pragmatic audit improvements: (1) sample provenance‑rich public items to exercise detector sensitivity to real web‑sourced leakage; (2) set independent_condition_generation = true so baseline and guarded conditions are produced by independent generations and cannot collapse to a shared output; (3) expand to multiple models and independent seeds to increase observable discordance and to allow cross‑model contamination signals; (4) record per‑item fuzzy overlap scores regardless of flag status so auditors can report overlap distributions even when thresholded flags are rare; and (5) apply paraphrase‑robust detectors and human adjudication for borderline cases. Each recommendation follows from artifacts: the execution manifest, deterministic_reconciliation, and analysis_log confirm the current run's settings and limits, and the contamination_summary artifact shows the empty flag set that motivates broader sampling and independent generation in future audits.

Operational implications. For NetOps practitioners, the audit demonstrates that audit sensitivity depends critically on sampling provenance and generation semantics. A contamination audit intended to assess public benchmark leakage should avoid synthetic provenance and shared generation semantics. Verifier‑backed validators remain valuable oracles for functional correctness checks, but auditor designs must ensure samples exercise detector capabilities and record detector outputs at a granularity sufficient for post‑hoc analysis.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, artifact‑anchored paired audit of conservative contamination detectors for LLM‑for‑NetOps evaluation. In the reproducible 150‑pair synthetic sample we observed zero preregistered high‑confidence contamination flags and identical validator pass rates (150/150 baseline, 150/150 guarded). The degenerate null outcome is artifact‑supported and stems from provenance‑stable synthetic sampling and shared generation semantics; it does not imply absence of contamination in web‑sourced benchmarks or failure of the preregistered detectors in different sampling regimes. We provide an explicit preregistration→execution reconciliation (archived artifacts and SHAs), confirm deterministic reconciliation checks passed, and recommend concrete design changes—provenance‑rich sampling, independent generation per condition, multi‑model scope, paraphrase‑sensitive detectors, and matched power calculations—to increase audit sensitivity in future studies. All experiment artifacts, validator traces, analysis inputs/outputs, and execution manifests are archived per the execution bundle and are available for verification as recorded in the Disclosure Statement below.

limitations: Single‑model execution (gpt‑5-mini) — results do not generalize across other LLM families, sizes, or training corpora.

Sampled items were provenance‑stable synthetic/deterministically generated tasks (source_identifier prefix "synthetic-netops:") for this run; absence of high‑confidence flags here may not reflect contamination prevalence in real‑world, web‑crawled benchmarks.

Generation semantics used shared_initial_candidate across baseline and guarded conditions (independent_condition_generation = false), producing identical model outputs when no exclusions occurred and thus limiting sensitivity to interventions that rely on independent re‑generation.

Contamination detection relied on preregistered conservative heuristics (exact match and fuzzy 5‑gram overlap thresholds); subtler contamination patterns (paraphrased memorization, partial leakage) may escape these heuristics and require richer provenance or manual adjudication.

Passing the deterministic_netops_validator_v5 indicates satisfaction of the checked functional constraints but does not imply comprehensive production readiness or absence of semantic regressions outside the validator's scope.
